title: K Emptiest Shelves
statement:
A warehouse rack is described by a grid shelves of 0 and 1. Each row is one shelf, and each 1 is a filled slot. Shelves are packed from the left, so in every row all the 1s come before all the 0s.

Shelf a is emptier than shelf b if it has fewer 1s, or the same number of 1s and a < b.

Return the row indexes of the k emptiest shelves, from the emptiest to the fullest.

examples.why: Rows 1 and 3 both hold one item. The tie is broken by the smaller row index, so 1 comes first.
Counts are 2, 0 and 1. All rows are returned, ordered by count, not by index.
Row 2 is the emptiest. Rows 0 and 1 tie for the next place, and row 0 wins the tie.

constraints: 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 100, the grid is m × n
shelves[i][j] is 0 or 1, with every row's 1s before its 0s
hints: First reduce each row to one number: how many 1s it has. Then the problem is ordering rows by (count, index).
Because the 1s come first, the count is the index of the first 0. A sorted-looking row invites binary search.
Sort the pairs (count, row) and take the first k, or keep a max-heap of size k so you never hold more than k candidates.

explain.intuition:
Each row only matters through one number, its count of 1s. Since every row is "ones, then zeros", that count is the position of the first 0, which binary search finds in O(log n) instead of scanning the row.

Ranking is then a sort by the pair (count, index). Comparing pairs handles the tie rule for free. To pick only k rows you can keep a max-heap of size k: push each row, and when the heap grows past k, pop the fullest. What remains are the k emptiest, which you read out in reverse.
steps: For each row, binary search for the first 0. Its index is the number of filled slots.
Push it into a max-heap ordered by the pair. If the heap holds more than k pairs, pop the largest.
Pop everything left: it comes out fullest first, so reverse it and return the row indexes.
pitfalls: Sorting by count only with an unstable sort, or forgetting the index tie-break when you write the comparator by hand.
Off-by-one in the binary search for a row that is all 1s: the answer must be n, not n − 1.
Returning the rows in index order instead of from the emptiest to the fullest.

complexity.time: O(m log n + m log k)

solutions.title: Count and sort
solutions.idea: Count the 1s of each row, sort the rows by (count, index) and keep the first k.

solutions.title: Binary search and a size-k max-heap
solutions.idea: Find each count with binary search, keep only the k emptiest rows in a max-heap, then read them out.
solutions.time: O(m log n + m log k)

followups: The rack has a million shelves but k is 5. Which version uses less memory, and why?
Rows are no longer packed from the left. Which part of the solution breaks, and what replaces it?
